status_note: Units 1-2 (VVER-1000, commercial 2014 and 2017) operate and units 3-6 are under construction. Spent fuel is held in the reactor pools; an additional away-from-reactor store is being built within the plant premises, to hold fuel until it is reprocessed.
operator: Nuclear Power Corporation of India Ltd (NPCIL)
notes: The construction status of the away-from-reactor (AFR) store is not confirmed.

name: Narora Atomic Power Station
status_note: Two PHWR units (IPHWR-220, commercial 1991 and 1992), both operating. Spent fuel is held in the on-site storage pool/bay.
operator: Nuclear Power Corporation of India Ltd (NPCIL)

name: Pokhran test range
status_note: Test area near Pokhran in the Thar Desert, Rajasthan; site of India's underground tests of 1974 (Smiling Buddha) and May 1998 (Pokhran-II).

name: Tarapur reprocessing complex (PREFRE, WIP and Solid Storage Surveillance Facility)
status_note: BARC's Tarapur site reprocesses PHWR fuel (PREFRE-2, 100 t/year, replacing the original PREFRE in 2010) and vitrifies high-level waste; the Solid Storage Surveillance Facility has stored vitrified waste for about 20 years. An Integrated Nuclear Recycle Plant to treble capacity was under construction in 2019.
operator: Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC), Department of Atomic Energy
notes: Position of the Tarapur power station; the BARC facilities are on the adjoining site. The power station is a separate entry.

name: Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant
status_note: One VVER-1000 unit (fuel loaded 2010, commercial operation 2013) operates; unit 2 is under construction. Under a 2005 agreement Russia supplies the fuel and spent fuel is to be returned to Russia.
notes: Whether any spent fuel has been returned to Russia is not confirmed; discharged fuel is assumed to be in the on-site pool.

name: Caorso nuclear power plant
status_note: One 860 MWe BWR, operated 1981-1990 and being decommissioned by Sogin. The 1,032 spent fuel assemblies were shipped to La Hague for reprocessing in 16 shipments between December 2007 and 2010.

name: EUREX plant, Saluggia
status_note: Former experimental reprocessing plant at Saluggia (Vercelli) under decommissioning by Sogin. About 260 m3 of liquid radioactive waste from past reprocessing, roughly 60% of the total radioactive waste activity in Italy (2015), are stored on site; the CEMEX plant is to solidify them and store the packages pending a national repository.
notes: Position of Saluggia, not the plant. The status of the CEMEX facility is not confirmed; classing the liquid waste as high-level is inferred from its share of national activity.

name: Garigliano nuclear power plant
status_note: One 150 MWe BWR, operated 1964-1978 (formally shut down 1982) and being decommissioned by Sogin. All fuel was removed from the pool: part went to Sellafield in 1987, the rest via the Avogadro store to La Hague in 2011. An interim store (DT2) for low- and intermediate-level waste is being built on site.

name: ITREC plant, Trisaia (Rotondella)
status_note: Former experimental fuel reprocessing plant in the ENEA Trisaia research centre, Rotondella (Matera), under decommissioning by Sogin. 64 spent uranium-thorium fuel elements from the US Elk River reactor are held in the plant's pool and are to be loaded into two dual-purpose casks and moved to the on-site DMC3/DTC3 store pending a national repository.
notes: Position of the ENEA Trisaia centre, within which ITREC lies. Whether the fuel has been loaded into casks is not confirmed.

name: Latina nuclear power plant
status_note: One 153 MWe Magnox reactor, operated 1963-1987 and being decommissioned by Sogin. Its Magnox spent fuel (about 1,400 t over its lifetime) was reprocessed at Sellafield in the UK.
notes: The unfinished CIRENE prototype on the same site never operated.

name: Trino (Enrico Fermi) nuclear power plant
status_note: One 260 MWe PWR, operated 1964-1990 and being decommissioned by Sogin. All spent fuel was sent abroad (UK and France) for reprocessing, the last of it in 2015.

name: Rokkasho Reprocessing Plant
status_note: Commercial reprocessing plant (800 tU/year design) under construction since 1993, with active tests from 2007; its spent fuel receiving pool already holds fuel from Japanese reactors. Completion was postponed for the 27th time to FY2026 (by March 2027), and in mid-2026 a 28th postponement was reported as certain.
notes: The latest delay is reported by an advocacy group (CNIC); no operator announcement confirms it.

name: Fugen Prototype Advanced Thermal Reactor
status_note: Prototype heavy-water-moderated ATR (148 MWe), operated 1979-2003 and now being decommissioned. Its 731 used fuel assemblies (about 111 t) are contracted for shipment to Orano's La Hague plant for reprocessing; shipments were planned for 2023-2026 but have been delayed.
notes: Assumes the fuel is still on site; no source confirms a shipment to France as of November 2026. Fugen and Tsuruga form a dual site.

name: Fukushima Daiichi accident site (melted fuel debris and treated-water tanks)
status_note: Three reactors melted down after the tsunami of 11 March 2011; an estimated 880 t of fuel debris remains in units 1-3, of which only gram-scale samples had been retrieved by 2024. Contaminated water is treated (ALPS) and stored in on-site tanks; diluted discharge to the sea began on 24 August 2023 and is expected to take decades. Decommissioning is expected to take 30-40 years.
notes: Figures are from Wikipedia, not from operator documents.

name: Fukushima Daini Nuclear Power Plant
status_note: Four BWR units (commercial 1982-1987), not operated since 2011; TEPCO decided in July 2019 to decommission all four (formally retired 30 September 2019). Spent fuel remains in the unit pools; the decommissioning plan foresees moving it to on-site dry cask storage.

name: Fukushima Interim Storage Facility for removed soil (Okuma and Futaba)
status_note: About 1,600 ha site in Okuma and Futaba around the Fukushima Daiichi plant that stores soil and waste from off-site decontamination: about 14.09 million m3 had been brought in by the end of March 2025. Japanese law requires final disposal outside Fukushima Prefecture by March 2045; about three quarters is below 8,000 Bq/kg and intended for reuse.
notes: Position of Futaba town; the facility surrounds the Fukushima Daiichi plant in both Okuma and Futaba. The 3/4 reuse share is not confirmed.

name: Genkai Nuclear Power Plant
status_note: Units 1 and 2 (PWR, 1975 and 1981) were retired in 2015 and 2019; units 3 and 4 (1994, 1997) operate. Spent fuel is held in the on-site pools.

name: Hamaoka Nuclear Power Plant
status_note: Five BWR/ABWR units: units 1 and 2 were shut down in 2009 and are being dismantled (unit 2 reactor dismantling began March 2025); units 3-5 have been idle since 2011, with the restart review of units 3 and 4 still ongoing in 2026. Spent fuel is held in the unit pools.

name: Higashidori Nuclear Power Plant (Tohoku)
status_note: One BWR (Tohoku unit 1, commercial 2005), idle since 2011 and under regulatory review; the adjacent TEPCO Higashidori unit 1 was never completed or fuelled. The unit's spent fuel is held in its on-site pool.

name: Horonobe Underground Research Center (JAEA)
status_note: Underground research laboratory in sedimentary rock in Hokkaido for geological disposal research, with galleries at 140, 250 and 350 m and a 500 m level planned. Research has been extended to FY2028, after which the site is to be backfilled; no radioactive waste is stored there.
source_urls: https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/幌延深地層研究センター

name: Ikata Nuclear Power Plant
status_note: Units 1 and 2 (PWR, 1977 and 1982) were retired in 2016 and 2018; unit 3 (1994) operates. An on-site dry cask store was being built, with the first 15 casks (for units 1-2 fuel) ordered and a start of operation planned for around July 2025.
notes: Whether the dry storage facility entered service in 2025 is not confirmed.

name: Kashiwazaki-Kariwa Nuclear Power Plant
status_note: Seven BWR/ABWR units (commercial 1985-1997), the largest nuclear site by capacity; unit 6 restarted in January 2026 and returned to commercial operation in April 2026, unit 7 has restart approval, units 1-5 are idle. Spent fuel is held in the unit pools.

name: Mihama Nuclear Power Plant
status_note: Units 1 and 2 (PWR, 1970 and 1972) were retired in March 2015 and are being decommissioned; unit 3 (1976) operates. Spent fuel is held in the pools; Kansai Electric plans an on-site dry storage facility (about 100 t) by around 2030.

name: Monju Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor
status_note: Prototype sodium-cooled fast breeder reactor; first criticality 1994, barely operated after a 1995 sodium leak, closure decided December 2016. As part of decommissioning (planned to 2047), all fuel was moved from the reactor to the on-site storage pool by 13 October 2022.

name: Ohi Nuclear Power Plant
status_note: Units 1 and 2 (PWR, 1979) were retired in December 2017; units 3 and 4 (1991, 1993) operate. Spent fuel is held in the pools; Kansai Electric plans an on-site dry storage facility (about 250 t) by around 2030.

name: Onagawa Nuclear Power Plant
status_note: Three BWR units: unit 1 (1984) was retired in 2018 and is being decommissioned, unit 2 (1995) has restarted and operates, unit 3 (2002) is idle. Spent fuel is held in the on-site pools.

name: Recyclable-Fuel Storage Center, Mutsu (RFS)
status_note: Japan's first away-from-reactor dry cask store for spent fuel, in Sekine, Mutsu, Aomori; capacity 3,000 t (5,000 t planned), storage for up to 50 years before reprocessing at Rokkasho. The first cask arrived from Kashiwazaki-Kariwa on 26 September 2024 and operation began on 6 November 2024; in 2026 the Aomori governor said he would not accept further deliveries for now.
operator: Recyclable-Fuel Storage Company (TEPCO 80 %, Japan Atomic Power 20 %)
source_urls: https://world-nuclear-news.org/articles/japanese-used-nuclear-fuel-store-starts-operating | https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/リサイクル燃料備蓄センター | https://cnic.jp/english/?p=9307 | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mutsu,_Aomori
notes: Position of Mutsu city; the facility (Oaza Sekine) lies several km away.

name: Rokkasho Low-Level Radioactive Waste Disposal Center (JNFL)
status_note: Near-surface concrete-pit disposal centre for low-level waste drums from Japanese nuclear power plants. No. 1 facility since December 1992, No. 2 since October 2000; the No. 3 facility was permitted in July 2021. About 330,000 drums were buried by 2022.
notes: Shares the Rokkasho reprocessing plant position; the disposal centre lies a few km away within the JNFL area.

name: Rokkasho Vitrified Waste Storage Center (JNFL)
status_note: Store with capacity for 2,880 canisters of vitrified high-level waste from reprocessing of Japanese fuel abroad: 1,310 canisters returned from France (1995-2007) and 520 from the UK by 2016. Canisters are kept for 30 to 50 years pending a geological repository.
notes: Shares the Rokkasho plant position (same JNFL site). The newest canister count found dates from 2016.

name: Sendai Nuclear Power Plant
status_note: Two PWR units (commercial 1984 and 1985), both operating; in 2015 they were the first Japanese reactors to restart under the post-Fukushima rules. Spent fuel is held in the on-site pools.

name: Shika Nuclear Power Plant
status_note: Two BWR/ABWR units (commercial 1993 and 2006), both idle since 2011; unit 2 is under restart review. Spent fuel is held in the on-site pools.

name: Shimane Nuclear Power Plant
status_note: Unit 1 (BWR, 1974) was retired in 2015 and is being decommissioned; unit 2 (1989) restarted on 7 December 2024; unit 3 (ABWR) is still under construction and has not been fuelled. Spent fuel is held in the pools.

name: Takahama Nuclear Power Plant
status_note: Four PWR units (commercial 1974-1985), all restarted and operating. Spent fuel is held in the pools; Kansai Electric plans an on-site dry storage facility (about 350 t) by around 2030.

name: Tokai Nuclear Power Station (Tokai-1 and Tokai No. 2)
status_note: Tokai-1 (Magnox, 1966-1998) is being decommissioned and its spent fuel pool was emptied and cleaned in 2001; Tokai No. 2 (BWR, 1978) has been idle since 2011 and has restart approval but remains offline. Besides its pool, Tokai No. 2 has had an on-site dry metal cask store in use since September 2001 (24-cask capacity).
notes: The cask capacity figure is from conference abstracts only.

name: Tokai Reprocessing Plant (JAEA)
status_note: Japan's first reprocessing plant (hot operation from 1977, full operation 1981, utility reprocessing ended 2006). The NRA approved its decommissioning plan in June 2018 (about 70 years). Vitrification of the remaining high-level liquid waste was delayed in December 2023 to between FY2035 and FY2038.
notes: Intermediate- and low-level waste (e.g. bituminised waste) is inferred from the 1997 asphalt facility fire, not from an inventory.

name: Tomari Nuclear Power Plant
status_note: Three PWR units (commercial 1989, 1991, 2009), all idle since 2012; unit 3 was cleared for restart by the regulator in 2025 with a restart targeted for 2027, units 1 and 2 remain under review. Spent fuel is held in the on-site pools.

name: Tsuruga Nuclear Power Plant
status_note: Unit 1 (BWR, 1970) was retired in 2015 and is being decommissioned; unit 2 (PWR, 1987) has been idle since 2011, and in November 2024 the regulator found it non-compliant because an active fault below the reactor could not be ruled out. Spent fuel is held in the on-site pools.
notes: Directly adjacent to the Fugen prototype reactor (separate entry, different operator).

name: Mailuu-Suu uranium tailings
status_note: Soviet uranium mining and milling from 1946 to 1968 left 23 tailings deposits on landslide-prone slopes above the town and the Mailuu-Suu River, upstream of the Fergana Valley. A tailings dam failure in 1958 released about 600,000 m3; the World Bank funded reclamation of tailings pits from 2004 and 2011, but risks remain.

name: Kiritimati (Christmas Island) nuclear test area
status_note: Base for the British Grapple H-bomb tests (1957-1958), including the Grapple X H-bomb detonated over the south-eastern tip of the island on 8 November 1957, and for the US Dominic series in 1962 (about 24 Mt). The population was not evacuated.
notes: Position of the Grapple X burst point. Air bursts left little local waste; residual contamination at the base is not documented.

name: Malden Island (Grapple 1-3 test area)
status_note: Site of the first British hydrogen bomb tests, Grapple 1-3, between 15 May and 19 June 1957, with Kiritimati as the main base. The uninhabited island is now a wildlife sanctuary.

name: Punggye-ri nuclear test site
status_note: North Korea's only known test site, with six underground tests from 2006 to 2017 in tunnels in mountainous terrain about 2 km south of Mantapsan. Tunnel entrances were demolished in May 2018, but the site was reported to have been restored in 2022.

name: Wolseong Low- and Intermediate-Level Radioactive Waste Disposal Center, Gyeongju
status_note: South Korea's only LILW disposal site, in Bongil-ri, Munmu Daewang-myeon, Gyeongju. Phase 1 is an underground silo facility (six silos, 100,000 drums) with first disposal on 13 July 2015, 37.7 % full by May 2026. The Phase 2 near-surface vault facility (125,000 drums) was completed on 13 May 2026 for operation from the second half of 2026; a Phase 3 landfill for very low-level waste is planned for 2031.
notes: Position of Bonggil-ri village, where the centre lies. Phase 1 is an underground silo (80-130 m below sea level), phase 2 near-surface; very-low-level refers to the planned phase 3.

name: Hanbit Nuclear Power Plant (Yeonggwang)
status_note: Six PWR units (commercial 1986-2002), all operating. Spent fuel is held in the unit pools.

name: Hanul Nuclear Power Plant (incl. Shin Hanul)
status_note: Hanul 1-6 (commercial 1988-2005) and Shin Hanul 1-2 (APR-1400, 2022 and 2024) operate; Shin Hanul 3-4 are under construction. Spent fuel is held in the unit pools.
notes: Includes the adjacent Shin Hanul units.

name: Kori Nuclear Power Plant (incl. Shin Kori and Saeul)
status_note: Kori 1 (1978) was shut down in 2017 and its decommissioning was approved, with its fuel to move from the pool to an on-site dry store planned for 2031; Kori 2-4, Shin Kori 1-2 and Saeul 1-2 (formerly Shin Kori 3-4) operate and Saeul 3-4 are under construction. All spent fuel is held in the unit pools.
notes: Includes Shin Kori and Saeul, which form one contiguous coastal site with Kori. The point marks the Kori units.

name: Wolsong Nuclear Power Plant (incl. Shin Wolsong)
status_note: Wolsong 1 (CANDU, 1983) was shut down on 24 December 2019; Wolsong 2-4 (CANDU) and Shin Wolsong 1-2 (PWR) operate. CANDU fuel moves after six years in pools to on-site dry storage (MACSTOR/KN-400 modules, seven built in 2010, seven more approved in January 2020 as the store neared capacity).
notes: Includes the adjacent Shin Wolsong units. Older canister and silo dry storage is not described in the sources; only MACSTOR is.

name: BN-350 fast reactor, Aktau
status_note: Sodium-cooled fast reactor that produced power and desalinated water at Aktau (formerly Shevchenko) from 1973 to 1999 and is being decommissioned. Its spent fuel was stored on site until 2009-10, when it was moved in dual-purpose casks to a store on the former Semipalatinsk test site near Kurchatov.
notes: The decommissioning operator is not confirmed.

name: Baikal-1 research reactor complex, long-term storage of BN-350 spent fuel
status_note: Long-term storage area at the Baikal-1 complex on the former Semipalatinsk test site, commissioned at the end of 2009; in 2010 sixty TUK-123 metal-concrete casks with spent fuel from the BN-350 fast reactor at Aktau were placed there for about 50 years.
operator: National Nuclear Center of the Republic of Kazakhstan (NNC RK)

name: Semipalatinsk Test Site (the Polygon)
status_note: Main Soviet nuclear test site: 456-468 tests (1949-1989), over 100 in the atmosphere, on an 18,000 km2 steppe area. Closed on 29 August 1991; plutonium left in tunnels and boreholes at Degelen and elsewhere was secured in a joint Kazakh-Russian-US operation between 1996 and 2012. Contamination remains at Ground Zero, Balapan (Chagan lake) and Degelen.
operator: National Nuclear Center of the Republic of Kazakhstan
notes: Sources differ on the number of tests (456 or 468). The point is nominal; the test site area is very large.

name: Ignalina Near Surface Repository (B25) for short-lived LILW
status_note: Near-surface vault repository next to the Ignalina NPP for short-lived low- and intermediate-level operational and decommissioning waste, designed for 300 years of institutional control. Construction started with a ceremony in November 2025; completion is reported for the end of 2028.
notes: The exact repository location is not published; the plant position is used. The end-2028 completion date is not confirmed.

name: Ignalina nuclear power plant (incl. interim spent fuel stores)
status_note: Two RBMK-1500 units, closed in December 2004 and at the end of 2009, now being decommissioned. Spent fuel was first stored in dry casks on site and was moved from the reactor pools to the new interim spent fuel storage facility (ISFSF) about 1 km from the plant, completed in April 2022; solid waste treatment and storage facilities are adjacent.
notes: Position of the plant; the interim spent fuel store lies about 1 km away.

name: Radioactive Waste Repository 'Radons', Baldone
status_note: Latvia's near-surface repository for low- and intermediate-level waste, about 5 km from Baldone and 27 km from Riga, operating since 1962. It holds waste from the dismantled Salaspils research reactor, industry and medicine, plus a significant share of Soviet-era defence-related waste.
operator: Latvian Environment, Geology and Meteorology Centre (LVĢMC)
notes: Position of Baldone town; the repository is about 5 km away. Continued operation is assumed from 2014-2015 sources; tritium in groundwater has been reported but not confirmed.

name: Bikini Atoll nuclear test site
status_note: The United States carried out 23 nuclear tests at Bikini between 1946 and 1958 (about 77 Mt), including Castle Bravo in 1954. Islanders who returned in 1972 were evacuated again in 1978 because of high caesium and strontium levels; the atoll remains unfit for resettlement.

name: Enewetak Atoll nuclear test site
status_note: US nuclear tests with a combined yield of over 30 Mt took place at Enewetak during the Cold War The 1977-1980 clean-up collected debris into the Runit Dome, but lagoon sediments and soils around the dome remain contaminated.

name: Runit Dome (Cactus Dome), Enewetak Atoll
status_note: Concrete cap 115 m across over the Cactus test crater on Runit Island, built 1977-1980 to hold about 73,000-76,000 m3 of contaminated soil and debris from the US nuclear tests at Enewetak (1946-1958). The crater floor is unlined and the dome is monitored by the US DOE; a 2020 DOE report found no immediate risk of breach.

name: Laguna Verde Nuclear Power Station
status_note: Two BWR units in operation; licences extended to 2050 (Unit 1) and 2055 (Unit 2). Spent fuel is held in the re-racked pools and, since 2016, in an on-site Holtec HI-STORM dry storage ISFSI with space for 130 casks.

name: COMINAK Akouta uranium mine (closure and remediation)
status_note: Underground uranium mine at Akouta near Arlit that produced more than 75,000 tU before closing on 31 March 2021 after depletion. Remediation of the mine workings, mill, tailings pile and ponds is expected to take at least ten years, followed by at least five years of monitoring.
notes: Position of Arlit town; Akouta lies nearby. The neighbouring SOMAIR open-pit mine and its tailings are not included.

name: Borssele nuclear power station
status_note: One PWR unit, grid-connected in 1973; the government plans to extend operation beyond 2033. Spent fuel is cooled in the plant pool and sent to La Hague for reprocessing; the returned high-level waste is stored at COVRA's HABOG next to the plant.
notes: The COVRA/HABOG central store is a separate entry.

name: COVRA central storage site incl. HABOG (Vlissingen-Oost)
status_note: Central Dutch radioactive waste site in the Sloegebied port area near Nieuwdorp (Borsele): HABOG stores high-level waste, LOG low- and intermediate-level waste, VOG depleted uranium and COG NORM from the phosphate industry. Waste is to be stored for about 100 years before geological disposal; HABOG is being expanded to hold all high-level waste until the Borssele plant closes.
notes: Spent fuel is listed because HABOG is known to hold research reactor spent fuel, but the COVRA source does not mention it. The 2003 opening year is not confirmed.

name: Dodewaard nuclear power plant
status_note: Small natural-circulation BWR (55-58 MWe), operated 1969-1997 and in safe enclosure, with demolition planned for 2045. The spent fuel was removed and reprocessed at Sellafield; the resulting waste is stored at COVRA in Borssele.

name: Halden research reactor site
status_note: Site of the Halden boiling heavy water research reactor, permanently shut down in June 2018. Norwegian Nuclear Decommissioning took over the licence on 1 April 2025 to decommission it; Norway's research reactor spent fuel (about 16.5 t in total, held at Halden and Kjeller) is to be shipped to Studsvik in Sweden under a 2026 agreement.
notes: Position of the IFE Halden office; the reactor hall is in the rock nearby. Sources do not split the fuel between Halden and Kjeller; Kjeller is not included.

name: Himdalen combined storage and disposal facility (KLDRA Himdalen)
status_note: Norway's combined storage and disposal facility for low- and intermediate-level waste in rock caverns at Himdalen (Aurskog-Høland). Disposal has been stopped; the regulator DSA ordered a periodic safety review in 2023 and is handling a permit to store waste already placed there, and the licence is being transferred from IFE to Norwegian Nuclear Decommissioning (NND).
operator: Institute for Energy Technology (IFE); transfer to Norwegian Nuclear Decommissioning (NND) pending
notes: Rock caverns in a hillside. Waste is held and managed here, but disposal operations have stopped.

name: Fangataufa Atoll nuclear test site
status_note: Uninhabited atoll owned by the French state since 1964; 4 atmospheric and 10 underground French nuclear tests were carried out here between 1966 and 1996, including the last French test on 27 January 1996.
operator: French Ministry of the Armed Forces

name: Moruroa Atoll nuclear test site
status_note: France carried out about 175-181 nuclear tests at Moruroa between 1966 and 1996 (41 atmospheric, the rest underground in shafts beneath the atoll). The test site was dismantled after 1996; the atoll remains closed and guarded by the French armed forces, with radiological and geomechanical monitoring.
operator: French Ministry of the Armed Forces
notes: Monitoring details and operator are from Wikipedia only.

name: Chashma Nuclear Power Plant
status_note: Four CNP-300 PWR units (C-1 to C-4, commercial 2000-2017) operate and C-5 (Hualong One) has been under construction since December 2024. Spent fuel is held on site.
notes: The spent fuel stores are not described in detail in the sources.

name: Karachi Nuclear Power Plant (KANUPP)
status_note: K-1 (CANDU, 1972) was shut down on 1 August 2021 and received a decommissioning licence in June 2022 (deferred dismantling); its spent fuel is managed in an on-site dry storage facility covered by that licence. K-2 and K-3 (Hualong One, 2021 and 2022) operate.
notes: Whether all K-1 fuel has been moved from the pool to the dry store is not confirmed.

name: Ras Koh Hills test site (Chagai-I)
status_note: Site of Pakistan's five simultaneous underground tests (Chagai-I) on 28 May 1998 at Koh Kambaran in the Ras Koh Hills, Chagai District, Balochistan. A further test (Chagai-II) followed on 30 May 1998.
notes: Whether the Chagai-II test took place in the Ras Koh Hills is not confirmed.

name: National Radioactive Waste Repository (KSOP), Różan
status_note: Surface disposal facility in a former Russian military fort (1905-1908) at Różan, operating since 1961 for short-lived low- and intermediate-level waste, and also used for temporary storage of long-lived waste. A replacement surface repository (NSPOP) is being sited; in July 2026 the ministry reopened the call for host municipalities until the end of 2027.
notes: Position of Różan town; the fort lies on its edge. Remaining capacity and closure date are not published.

name: Cernavodă nuclear power plant
status_note: Two CANDU-6 units (unit 1 in commercial operation since December 1996). Spent fuel cools at the reactors for six to ten years and is then moved to the on-site dry storage facility DICA (Macstor design) for about 50 years; an intermediate-level waste store is under construction.

name: National Repository for Low and Intermediate Level Waste (DNDR) Băița, Bihor
status_note: Repository in galleries of an exhausted uranium mine at Băița in the Apuseni Mountains, in operation since 1985 for institutional low- and intermediate-level waste. Designed for about 21,000 drums, of which more than 6,000 (about 30%) had been disposed of according to the operator.
operator: IFIN-HH (Horia Hulubei National Institute for Physics and Nuclear Engineering)
notes: Position of the Băița uranium mine, of which the repository gallery is part; its portal is not published. The fill level is from an undated source.

name: Mayak Production Association (RT-1 reprocessing plant and waste stores), Ozyorsk
status_note: Former plutonium production complex near Ozyorsk whose RT-1 plant reprocesses civil, research, naval and production-reactor fuel (nominal 400 t/yr, historically 110-130 t/yr; 993 t in 2016-2024). It holds large stocks of high-level waste; the EP-500 vitrification furnace ran from 2016 to 2020 and successor melters are under development. Historic discharges contaminated the Techa River and Lake Karachay.
notes: 'Transuranic' reflects plutonium handling. The Kyshtym 1957 accident is a separate entry.

name: Novaya Zemlya Test Site, Zone A (Chernaya Guba, southern test area)
status_note: Southern test area of the Soviet Arctic test site, used for atmospheric, surface and underwater tests from 1955 to 1962 and for underground tests from 1972 to 1975. Novaya Zemlya hosted 224 nuclear detonations in total (about 265 Mt).
operator: Ministry of Defence of the Russian Federation
notes: Zone position rounded to 0.1°; individual test locations are not mapped. Russia carries out subcritical experiments at Zone B, and satellite imagery since 2023 shows new construction.

name: Abrosimov Fjord dumped reactor compartments (Novaya Zemlya)
status_note: In 1965 the Soviet Navy dumped reactor compartments from nuclear submarines (factory numbers 285 and 901), some with spent fuel, in this shallow fjord on the east coast of Novaya Zemlya at about 20 m depth, along with containers of solid waste. Russian-Norwegian surveys located the compartments in the 1990s.
notes: IAEA revised activity for the two compartments with fuel: 11.6 and 2.9 PBq at the time of dumping. Published coordinates are slightly inaccurate.

name: Akademik Lomonosov floating nuclear power plant, Pevek
status_note: Floating plant with two KLT-40S reactors, in commercial operation at Pevek (Chukotka) since December 2019. It is refuelled on site every three to four years; spent fuel is kept on board until the vessel returns to a shipyard for overhaul at the end of a 12-year cycle.
notes: On-board storage of spent fuel between refuellings is inferred, not stated directly.

name: Andreeva Bay former naval spent fuel and waste storage site (Zapadnaya Litsa)
status_note: Former Northern Fleet shore base about 60 km north-west of Murmansk that once held about 22,000 spent naval fuel assemblies in degraded stores plus solid and liquid waste. Fuel removal began in 2017; more than half had been shipped by late 2024, but progress slowed after international funding stopped in 2022 and completion has slipped into the 2030s.
notes: Waste classes for solid and liquid waste are not specified in detail.

name: Balakovo nuclear power plant
status_note: Four VVER-1000 units (grid-connected 1985-1993). Spent fuel is kept at the plant for at least three years and then shipped to the central stores and reprocessing plants (Mayak RT-1 or the Mining and Chemical Combine at Zheleznogorsk).
notes: Storage practice is described from the general Russian fuel cycle, not from plant-specific sources.

name: Beloyarsk nuclear power plant
status_note: Fast reactors BN-600 (unit 3, from 1980) and BN-800 (unit 4, from 2015) in operation; the early graphite units AMB-100 and AMB-200 were shut down in 1983 and 1990. BN-600 spent fuel has historically gone to Mayak for reprocessing; fuel is held on site for at least three years first.
notes: Whether AMB spent fuel is still stored on site is not confirmed.

name: Bilibino nuclear power plant
status_note: Four small EGP-6 graphite-moderated units in Chukotka; unit 1 shut down in 2018 and units 2-4 in December 2025. The spent fuel is stored at the Bilibino site.

name: Blagopoluchiye Inlet solid radioactive waste dumping area (Novaya Zemlya)
status_note: Inlet on the east coast of northern Novaya Zemlya (13-16 m depth) used by the Soviet Union for solid radioactive waste; about 8.7 TBq reported.

name: East Urals Radioactive Trace (Kyshtym 1957) and East Ural Nature Reserve
status_note: The explosion of a high-level liquid waste tank at Mayak on 29 September 1957 (INES 6) spread hot particles over more than 52,000 km2; about 10,000 people were evacuated. The most contaminated part is the East Ural Nature Reserve (166 km2, established 1968), a restricted 'radiation reserve' monitored by Rosatom.
notes: Sources differ on area figures. 'Closed' means restricted and monitored, not cleaned up.

name: Gremikha former naval base spent fuel store
status_note: Northern Fleet base on the eastern Kola coast that serviced liquid-metal-cooled submarine reactors; transferred to the nuclear ministry in 2000. All spent uranium-beryllium fuel (over 90% enriched) was removed in 11 consignments to Mayak, the last in November 2024. The remaining waste and the state of site clean-up are not documented.
notes: Spent fuel is listed as the former inventory; the last fuel was removed in November 2024. Residual waste and the state of clean-up are not documented.

name: K-159 (sunken Soviet nuclear submarine, Barents Sea)
status_note: The decommissioned November-class submarine, never defuelled, sank under tow on 30 August 2003 in the Barents Sea at about 200 m depth with an estimated 800 kg of spent fuel; nine crew died. A 2020 Russian draft decree proposed raising K-159 and K-27.
notes: The position lies inside the Russian maritime boundary. The status of salvage plans after 2020 is not known.

name: Kalinin nuclear power plant
status_note: Four VVER-1000 units (grid-connected 1984-2011). Spent fuel is kept at the plant for at least three years and then shipped to the central stores and reprocessing plants (Mayak RT-1 or the Mining and Chemical Combine at Zheleznogorsk).
notes: Storage practice is described from the general Russian fuel cycle, not from plant-specific sources.

name: Kola nuclear power plant
status_note: Four VVER-440 units (grid-connected 1973-1984), licensed to between 2026 and 2039. Spent VVER-440 fuel is held on site for at least three years and then sent to the Mayak RT-1 plant for reprocessing.
notes: Storage practice is described from the general Russian fuel cycle, not from plant-specific sources.

name: Kursk nuclear power plant (incl. Kursk II)
status_note: Four RBMK-1000 units: unit 1 shut down in December 2021 and unit 2 in January 2024, units 3-4 operate; the first VVER-TOI unit of the adjacent Kursk II was grid-connected in December 2025. Spent RBMK fuel has accumulated in on-site stores and is being transferred to centralised dry storage at Zheleznogorsk.
notes: Includes Kursk II, about 2 km away. Storage practice is described from the general Russian fuel cycle, not from plant-specific sources.

name: Lake Karachay (Mayak waste reservoir V-9)
status_note: Small lake used from 1951 to receive liquid high-level waste from Mayak, accumulating about 4.4 EBq; wind-blown dust spread contamination in 1968. Concrete blocks were placed from 1978 to 1986, the lake was fully backfilled in November 2015 and covering was completed in December 2016; groundwater monitoring continues.
notes: Activity figure from the Worldwatch Institute (via Wikipedia); the operator is not confirmed.

name: Leningrad Radon storage and disposal site (former RosRAO Leningrad branch), Sosnovy Bor
status_note: Regional 'Radon' combine branch at Sosnovy Bor, founded in 1961, collecting, processing and storing radioactive waste from north-west Russia; its repository was extended with a new solid waste facility of about 5,000 m2.
operator: Rosatom radioactive waste enterprise (former RosRAO), Leningrad branch
notes: Position of Sosnovy Bor town; the site location is not published. Whether waste is disposed of, not only stored, is not confirmed.

name: Leningrad nuclear power plant (incl. Leningrad II), Sosnovy Bor
status_note: Four RBMK-1000 units: unit 1 shut down in December 2018 and unit 2 in November 2020 (defuelled by 2021 and 2024), units 3-4 operate; the two VVER-1200 units of Leningrad II entered operation in 2018 and 2020, with two more under construction. Spent RBMK fuel has accumulated in on-site stores and is being transferred to centralised dry storage at Zheleznogorsk.
notes: Includes the adjacent Leningrad II. Storage practice is described from the general Russian fuel cycle, not from plant-specific sources.

name: Mining and Chemical Combine (MCC/GKhK) centralised spent fuel storage, Zheleznogorsk
status_note: Russia's central store for spent RBMK-1000 and VVER-1000 fuel: a wet pool store plus a dry store whose first stage opened in 2011-2012; the full dry store is designed for about 38,000 t. Loading of RBMK fuel into dry store building 3 began in March 2025; storage for at least 50 years pending a decision on reprocessing.
notes: Position of the combine; the storage buildings are part of the complex. Kozloduy spent fuel was also sent here.

name: Mining and Chemical Combine, former plutonium production complex (Krasnoyarsk-26), Zheleznogorsk
status_note: Underground plutonium production complex with three reactors cooled by Yenisei river water (started 1958-1965); the last reactor, ADE-2, was shut down in 2010 under the plutonium agreement with the US. The site now also hosts MOX fuel fabrication for the BN-800.
notes: Waste types are generic for a production complex; deep-well injection and river contamination are not covered by the sources.

name: NO RAO near-surface disposal facility for class 3-4 waste, Ozersk
status_note: Near-surface final disposal facility for solid class 3 and 4 (low- and intermediate-level) waste, mainly from Mayak, built by the national operator NO RAO. As of March 2026 it was under construction with the first stage scheduled for commissioning in 2026.
operator: NO RAO (National Operator for Radioactive Waste Management), Ozersk branch
notes: Exact site not published; the Mayak position is used as a stand-in. Whether commissioning took place in 2026 is not confirmed.

name: NO RAO near-surface disposal facility for class 3-4 waste, Seversk
status_note: Near-surface final disposal facility for solid class 3 and 4 waste being built by NO RAO at Seversk. As of March 2026 the first stage was scheduled for commissioning in 2026.
operator: NO RAO (National Operator for Radioactive Waste Management), Seversk branch
notes: Exact site not located; the town position is used. First waste was planned for summer 2026; this is not confirmed.

name: NO RAO near-surface disposal facility, Novouralsk
status_note: Russia's first near-surface final disposal facility for solid class 3 and 4 waste, in reinforced concrete structures; first waste (13 packages, 47 m3) received in November 2016. Planned total capacity with later phases up to 55,000 m3; the operator reported ten years without radiation incidents in March 2026.
operator: NO RAO (National Operator for Radioactive Waste Management), Ural branch
notes: Position of Novouralsk town; the facility lies in the town area near the Ural Electrochemical Plant.

name: Novaya Zemlya Test Site, Zone B (Matochkin Shar, northern test area)
status_note: Northern underground test area on both sides of the Matochkin Strait, used for underground tests from 1964 to 1990; the last Soviet test (1990) was at Novaya Zemlya. Russia has carried out subcritical experiments here since 1998 and has expanded tunnels and buildings since 2013.
operator: Ministry of Defence of the Russian Federation
notes: Zone position rounded to 0.1°; individual test locations are not mapped. Russia carries out subcritical experiments at Zone B, and satellite imagery since 2023 shows new construction.

name: Novaya Zemlya Test Site, Zone C (Sukhoy Nos)
status_note: Atmospheric test area on the Sukhoy Nos peninsula used from 1958 to 1961, including the Tsar Bomba air burst of 30 October 1961.
notes: Zone position rounded to 0.1°; individual test locations are not mapped. Russia carries out subcritical experiments at Zone B, and satellite imagery since 2023 shows new construction.

name: Novovoronezh nuclear power plant (incl. Novovoronezh II)
status_note: Five early VVER units of which units 4 (VVER-440) and 5 (VVER-1000) still operate, plus two VVER-1200 units of Novovoronezh II (grid-connected 2016 and 2019). Spent fuel is kept at the plant for at least three years and then shipped to the central stores and reprocessing plants (Mayak RT-1 or the Mining and Chemical Combine at Zheleznogorsk).
notes: Includes the adjacent Novovoronezh II. Shutdown of units 1-3 is inferred; storage practice is from the general Russian fuel cycle, not plant-specific sources.

name: Oga Inlet solid radioactive waste dumping area (Novaya Zemlya)
status_note: Inlet on the east coast of Novaya Zemlya (about 24 m depth) used by the Soviet Union for solid radioactive waste; about 75 TBq reported.

name: Rostov nuclear power plant
status_note: Four VVER-1000 units (grid-connected 2001-2018). Spent fuel is kept at the plant for at least three years and then shipped to the central stores and reprocessing plants (Mayak RT-1 or the Mining and Chemical Combine at Zheleznogorsk).
notes: Storage practice is described from the general Russian fuel cycle, not from plant-specific sources.

name: Saida Bay long-term storage of submarine reactor compartments and regional waste conditioning centre
status_note: Onshore concrete pad for long-term storage of reactor compartments from decommissioned submarines (construction from 2004, design about 120 compartments); the last afloat compartment was brought ashore in August 2019. A regional centre for conditioning and long-term storage of low- and intermediate-level waste opened in 2015.
operator: SevRAO (northern branch of Rosatom's radioactive waste company)
notes: Position of Sayda-Guba; the pad is on the bay shore. Counts differ: about 110 compartments (2019) or at least 116.

name: Sedov Inlet solid radioactive waste dumping area (Novaya Zemlya)
status_note: Shallow inlet (13-33 m) on the east coast of Novaya Zemlya where the Soviet Union dumped solid radioactive waste in containers, ships and unpackaged form; at about 126 TBq it is the largest of the Arctic solid waste areas by reported activity.

name: Siberian Chemical Combine (SCC), Seversk
status_note: Former plutonium production and reprocessing complex (formerly Tomsk-7); the last production reactor shut down in 2008 and all reactors were decommissioned by 2023, while uranium enrichment and conversion continue. More than 30 million m3 of liquid low- and intermediate-level waste has been injected into deep wells; a 1993 tank explosion in the radiochemical plant released contamination.
notes: Position of Seversk town; the industrial site lies to its north. The site remains an active industrial complex although the production reactors are being decommissioned.

name: Smolensk nuclear power plant
status_note: Three RBMK-1000 units (grid-connected 1982-1990). Spent RBMK fuel has accumulated in on-site stores and is being transferred to centralised dry storage at Zheleznogorsk.
notes: Storage practice is described from the general Russian fuel cycle, not from plant-specific sources.

name: Stepovoy Fjord: scuttled submarine K-27 and solid waste
status_note: The Soviet experimental submarine K-27, with two liquid-metal-cooled reactors containing spent fuel, was scuttled in Stepovoy Fjord off Novaya Zemlya at about 30-50 m depth; solid waste containers were also dumped in the fjord. Russia has considered raising K-27 together with K-159.
notes: Sources differ on the year: 1981 (IAEA) or 6 September 1982 (Wikipedia). A Russian-Norwegian survey located the submarine at 72°31'33"N 55°33'50"E.

name: Techa River and reservoir cascade (Mayak discharges)
status_note: From 1949 to 1956 Mayak discharged about 76 million m3 of radioactive waste water (about 102 PBq) into the Techa River; 23 riverside villages were later evacuated. Contaminated sediments and floodplains remain along the river.
notes: Position on the upper Techa near Mayak. 'Abandoned' refers to the river floodplain, not the reservoir cascade.

name: Techeniye Inlet solid radioactive waste dumping area (Novaya Zemlya)
status_note: Inlet on the east coast of northern Novaya Zemlya (up to 50 m depth) used by the Soviet Union for solid radioactive waste; about 68 TBq reported.

name: Tsivolka Fjord: icebreaker Lenin reactor shielding assembly and solid waste
status_note: In 1967 the shielding assembly of a reactor from the nuclear icebreaker Lenin, still holding about 60% of its damaged fuel, was dumped in Tsivolka Fjord, Novaya Zemlya, at about 50 m depth, together with solid waste containers. IASAP estimated about 19.6 PBq at the time of dumping.

name: Yeniseisky underground research laboratory, Nizhnekansky massif
status_note: Underground research laboratory in granitoid gneiss of the Nizhnekansky massif at the Yeniseisky site of NO RAO's Zheleznogorsk branch, to test suitability for a deep repository for high-level and long-lived intermediate-level waste. Shaft sinking was under way by mid-2023; operation is planned for 2028.
operator: NO RAO (National Operator for Radioactive Waste Management), Zheleznogorsk branch
notes: No coordinates found; the laboratory lies next to the Mining and Chemical Combine at Zheleznogorsk, whose position is used.

name: Spent Fuel Repository, Forsmark (Slutförvaret för använt kärnbränsle)
status_note: Deep geological repository for spent fuel at about 500 m depth at Söderviken in the Forsmark industrial area, designed for about 12,000 t of spent fuel in more than 6,000 copper canisters. Ground was broken on 15 January 2025; underground construction is to follow, with disposal expected to start in the 2030s.
notes: The exact surface site (Söderviken) is not mapped; the point lies near the Forsmark plant.

name: Äspö Hard Rock Laboratory
status_note: SKB's underground research laboratory near Oskarshamn, reaching almost 500 m depth, used for full-scale tests of the copper canister, bentonite and rock system for the spent fuel repository. SKB states that no spent fuel is kept there.

name: SFR final repository for short-lived radioactive waste, Forsmark
status_note: Rock-cavern repository beneath the Baltic seabed off Forsmark for short-lived low- and intermediate-level operational waste, with about 63,000 m3 of capacity, roughly 60% full. An extension with six new vaults at 120-140 m depth for decommissioning waste (about 117,000 m3 more) has been under construction since rock excavation began in January 2025.

name: Barsebäck nuclear power plant
status_note: Two BWR units, closed in 1999 and 2005. Shortly after the 2005 shutdown all spent fuel was taken to Clab; reactor internals segmented in 2016-2019 are kept in a new on-site interim store, and a further store for low- and intermediate-level waste was applied for in 2019.

name: Clab central interim storage facility for spent nuclear fuel
status_note: Central wet store at Simpevarp, about 25 km north of Oskarshamn, operating since 1985: spent fuel from all Swedish reactors is kept in pools about 30 m underground. It is licensed for 11,000 t and held just over 8,000 t; SKB's encapsulation plant is being built next to it.

name: Forsmark nuclear power plant
status_note: Three BWR units in operation since the 1980s. Spent fuel is held in the reactor pools and then shipped to the central interim store Clab at Oskarshamn. The SFR repository for short-lived waste and the planned spent fuel repository are on neighbouring land.
notes: The Forsmark repositories are separate entries.

name: Oskarshamn nuclear power plant
status_note: Three BWR units: Oskarshamn 2 closed in December 2016 and unit 1 in June 2017; unit 3 operates. Spent fuel is cooled in the reactor pools and then moved to Clab, the central interim store for all Swedish spent fuel, located on the same site (separate entry).

name: Ringhals nuclear power plant
status_note: Four units: Ringhals 2 (PWR) closed in December 2019 and Ringhals 1 (BWR) in December 2020; Ringhals 3 and 4 (PWR, 1981/1983) operate. Spent fuel is held in the reactor pools and then shipped to the central interim store Clab at Oskarshamn.

name: Krško nuclear power plant
status_note: One PWR unit, jointly owned by Slovenia and Croatia. Spent fuel and operational low- and intermediate-level waste are stored on site; a Holtec dry storage facility was commissioned in April 2023, with 16 HI-STORM FW casks (592 assemblies) loaded in the first campaign.
notes: The nearby Vrbina repository is a separate entry.

name: Central Radioactive Waste Storage Facility Brinje (CSRAO)
status_note: Partly underground reinforced concrete store for institutional radioactive waste from medicine, industry and research, operating since 1999. Space is largely used up; waste meeting acceptance criteria is to go to the Vrbina repository. The operating licence was extended for ten years in 2018.
notes: Position of Brinje settlement; the store itself is not pinpointed. Waste levels are inferred from the description as institutional waste.

name: LILW Repository Vrbina (Odlagališče NSRAO), Krško
status_note: Silo-type disposal facility (about 27 m diameter, 56 m deep, 990 containers) for low- and intermediate-level waste from the Krško NPP and from Slovenian medicine, research and industry. Construction of the nuclear part began on 1 October 2024 after site preparation from August 2023; completion and trial operation are expected in 2027.
notes: No published coordinates; the point lies slightly east of the Krško plant, where the site is described.

name: Žirovski vrh uranium mine: Jazbec and Boršt disposal sites
status_note: The uranium mine, closed since 1990, deposited mine waste at Jazbec and hydrometallurgical mill tailings at Boršt. Both sites have been finally remediated and are under long-term environmental monitoring; the estimated dose from Boršt in 2022 was about 2.4 µSv per year for adults, about 0.25% of the public limit.
notes: Position of Todraž, seat of the mine; the Jazbec and Boršt sites lie nearby.

name: Mochovce nuclear power plant
status_note: VVER-440 units 1 and 2 (1998/1999) and unit 3 (grid-connected January 2023) operate; unit 4 is being completed. Spent fuel is held in the reactor pools; Slovakia's interim spent fuel store is at Bohunice. The national near-surface LILW repository is next to the plant (separate entry).

name: Interim Spent Fuel Storage Bohunice (MSVP), Jaslovské Bohunice
status_note: Central wet store (four pools, capacity 14,112 assemblies) at Jaslovské Bohunice receiving spent fuel from all Slovak reactors (Bohunice V-1/V-2, Mochovce). A dry storage extension built from 2021 received regulatory approval for early use and commissioning in January 2024.
notes: Located on the Bohunice plant site; listed as interim storage because it is the national central spent fuel store. Routine operation of the dry store is not confirmed.

name: Jaslovské Bohunice nuclear site (A1, V1, V2 and spent fuel store)
status_note: Site of the A1 prototype (damaged in a 1977 accident, its fuel returned to Russia by 1990), the two V1 units (shut down 2006 and 2008, being decommissioned by JAVYS) and the two operating V2 units. The national interim wet store for spent fuel (1680 t, since 1986) is here, and a dry storage extension for 10,115 assemblies entered operation in 2024.
operator: JAVYS (spent fuel store, V1, A1); Slovenské elektrárne (V2)
notes: The interim store on this site also receives fuel from Mochovce.

name: National Radioactive Waste Repository Mochovce (RÚ RAO)
status_note: Multi-barrier surface repository in the Mochovce area for conditioned low-level waste in fibre-concrete containers (three double rows, about 33,480 m3 built) plus very-low-level waste trenches opened in 2016 and 2017 for decommissioning waste from Bohunice A1 and V1. In operation since 2001; further rows and a third VLLW phase are to be built as needed.
notes: Position of the Mochovce plant; the repository is in the Mochovce area. Sources give 1999 or 2001 as the start of operation.

name: Taboshar (Istiqlol) uranium tailings
status_note: Site of the first Soviet uranium mine (Second World War). An 8 ha tailings dump holds about 1.12 million m3; in 2022 a contract was agreed for a TVEL subsidiary to reclaim it.
notes: Progress of the 2022 reclamation contract is not confirmed.

name: Chinshan (Jinshan) Nuclear Power Plant
status_note: Two BWR units (1978, 1979), permanently shut down and in decommissioning; both cores are now empty. The outdoor dry storage facility received its operating licence on 1 May 2025 (14 casks stored by July 2026); in October 2026 about 6,030 assemblies remained in the pools and 840 were in dry storage.
notes: Assessed by the ministry in November 2025 as not feasible to restart.

name: Kuosheng Nuclear Power Plant
status_note: Two BWR units, shut down on 1 July 2021 and 15 March 2023; one core is still loaded and about 9,500 assemblies are in the pools (October 2026). Its outdoor dry store, almost ten years behind schedule, is in pre-operational testing (plan approved March 2026), and a restart was judged feasible in November 2025.
notes: Official figures list 87 assemblies in dry storage although the facility is not yet licensed for operation, possibly from test loading.

name: Lanyu (Orchid Island) Low-Level Radioactive Waste Storage Site
status_note: Storage site on Orchid Island, home of the Tao people, that received 97,672 drums of low-level waste from 1982 until February 1996. The waste remains on the island; relocation has been promised since the 1990s but no disposal or central storage site exists, and residents receive compensation.
notes: 'Operating' means the store still holds waste under management; it has not accepted waste since 1996.

name: Maanshan Nuclear Power Plant
status_note: Two PWR units, shut down in July 2024 and on 17 May 2025 when their operating licences expired; the cores have been emptied and 3,785 assemblies are in the pools (October 2026). An indoor dry store is in the design stage; a restart was judged feasible in November 2025.

name: Vector Radioactive Waste Management Complex (Chornobyl Exclusion Zone)
status_note: Complex about 17 km from the Chornobyl NPP with an engineered near-surface disposal facility for solid waste, a reinforced-concrete container facility (SRW-1) and a bulk waste module (SRW-2), designed for about 300 years of isolation. The first 120 packages of conditioned ChNPP waste were accepted in September 2019; it is also meant to take waste from other Ukrainian NPPs and returned vitrified waste.
operator: SSE Central Enterprise for Radioactive Waste Management (CERWM)
notes: No published coordinates; the point is the former village of Buriakivka, in the same south-western part of the zone as the Vector site.

name: Chornobyl Exclusion Zone
status_note: About 2,600 km2 of the most contaminated land around the Chornobyl plant (accident of 1986), closed to settlement and managed by the State Agency of Ukraine on Exclusion Zone Management, which also runs radioactive waste storage and disposal there. The zone was occupied by Russian forces from 24 February to early April 2022 and remains closed to visitors under martial law.
operator: State Agency of Ukraine on Exclusion Zone Management
notes: The zone is an accident area, not a single facility; 'remediation' reflects ongoing waste management and monitoring, not a clean-up of the whole zone.

name: Buriakivka Radioactive Waste Disposal Site
status_note: Trench disposal site in the Chornobyl Exclusion Zone, commissioned in 1987 for low- and intermediate-level accident waste; 31 clay-lined trenches (150 x 50 m) are filled with about 636,000 m3 of waste, including contaminated vehicles. In August 2026 the regulator approved construction of a new trench, No. 11A.
operator: SSE Central Enterprise for Radioactive Waste Management (CERWM)
notes: Position of the resettled village of Buriakivka (about 12 km from the plant), after which the site is named.

name: Centralised Spent Fuel Storage Facility (CSFSF / TsSVYaP)
status_note: Holtec dry cask store in the south-western part of the Chornobyl Exclusion Zone for VVER spent fuel from the Rivne, Khmelnytskyi and South Ukraine NPPs, designed for 16,530 assemblies and 100 years. The first casks arrived in 2023 under a trial operation permit and Energoatom declared it fully operational in December 2023.
notes: A 50th cask milestone (May 2026) and a 100-year operating licence are reported but not confirmed.

name: Chornobyl Unit 4: Shelter (sarcophagus) and New Safe Confinement
status_note: The destroyed reactor 4 and its 1986 Shelter, with the remains of the core, are enclosed by the New Safe Confinement arch, completed in 2019. A drone strike on 14 February 2025 breached the arch's cladding; in December 2025 the IAEA found it had lost its primary confinement function, with temporary repairs planned for 2026.
notes: The operator and the status of the 2026 repairs are not confirmed.

name: Chornobyl nuclear power plant spent fuel stores (ISF-1 and ISF-2)
status_note: Four RBMK units: unit 4 was destroyed in 1986, unit 2 shut down in 1991, unit 1 in 1996 and unit 3 in 2000. Spent fuel from units 1-3 (over 21,000 assemblies) has been held in the wet store ISF-1 (since 1986) and is being transferred to the Holtec dry store ISF-2, which began receiving fuel in June 2021; ISF-1 is to be decommissioned once the transfer ends around 2030.
notes: Covers only the spent fuel stores on the plant site; the accident site is a separate entry.

name: Khmelnytskyi nuclear power plant
status_note: Two VVER-1000 units in operation; units 3 and 4 are unfinished. Spent fuel is held in the reactor pools; it was formerly shipped to Russia and since December 2023 goes to the Centralised Spent Fuel Storage Facility (CSFSF) in the Chornobyl exclusion zone.
notes: Shipment of fuel to the central store (CSFSF) is inferred from general sources, not plant-specific data.

name: Rivne nuclear power plant
status_note: Four units: two VVER-440 (Rivne 1-2) and two VVER-1000 (Rivne 3-4) in operation. Spent VVER-440 fuel historically went to Mayak in Russia. Spent fuel is held in the reactor pools; it was formerly shipped to Russia and since December 2023 goes to the Centralised Spent Fuel Storage Facility (CSFSF) in the Chornobyl exclusion zone.

name: South Ukraine nuclear power plant
status_note: Three VVER-1000 units in operation. Spent fuel is held in the reactor pools; it was formerly shipped to Russia and since December 2023 goes to the Centralised Spent Fuel Storage Facility (CSFSF) in the Chornobyl exclusion zone.

name: Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant (incl. dry spent fuel store)
status_note: Six VVER-1000 units, the largest plant in Europe; under Russian military occupation since March 2022, with all units in cold shutdown since September 2022. Spent fuel is held in the reactor pools and in an on-site long-term dry storage facility in operation since 2001.

name: Waste Isolation Pilot Plant (WIPP)
status_note: Deep repository in a salt formation about 655 m underground, roughly 26 miles south-east of Carlsbad, for defence transuranic waste. First waste arrived from Los Alamos in March 1999; operations resumed in 2017 after the 2014 incidents, and shipments continue (e.g. Idaho's 7,500th shipment in April 2025).
operator: Salado Isolation Mining Contractors (SIMCO) for the US Department of Energy

name: Yucca Mountain repository (proposed)
status_note: Site designated under the Nuclear Waste Policy Act for a spent fuel and high-level waste repository. DOE sought to withdraw its licence application in 2010; after a 2013 court order the NRC finished its safety evaluation (2015) and environmental supplement (2016), but the licensing hearing remains suspended and the project has had no funding since. It has not been legally cancelled.
notes: Dormant, not cancelled: the statutory designation stands and the NRC proceeding is suspended, not terminated. No waste was ever emplaced.

name: Indian Point Energy Center
status_note: All three PWR units are shut down (Unit 1 1962-1974, Unit 2 to 2020, Unit 3 to 2021) and being decommissioned. All spent fuel (3,998 assemblies in 127 casks) has been in the on-site dry storage ISFSI since October 2023.
operator: Holtec Decommissioning International (owner Holtec Indian Point 2 and 3, LLC)
notes: The licences were transferred from Entergy to Holtec (NRC order of 23 November 2020).

name: Amchitka Island underground test site
status_note: Three US underground tests: Long Shot (1965), Milrow (1969) and Cannikin (1971, about 5 Mt, the largest US underground test). The AEC left in 1973; DOE stabilised drilling mud pits in 2001 and the site is under long-term monitoring.
operator: US Department of Energy (Office of Legacy Management)

name: Arkansas Nuclear One
status_note: Two PWR units in operation (operating licences 1974 and 1978). Spent fuel is stored in the reactor pool(s) and in dry casks at an on-site ISFSI.

name: Barnwell Low-Level Radioactive Waste Disposal Facility
status_note: State-owned 235-acre shallow-land disposal site near Snelling, Barnwell County, in operation since 1971 and leased to EnergySolutions. Since 2008 it accepts Class A, B and C waste only from the Atlantic Compact states (South Carolina, New Jersey, Connecticut); in 2016 about 1 million cubic feet of capacity remained.
notes: Position of Snelling town; the facility position is not sourced. The newest status source dates from 2016.

name: Beaver Valley Power Station
status_note: Two PWR units in operation (operating licences 1976 and 1987). Spent fuel is stored in the reactor pool(s) and in dry casks at an on-site ISFSI.

name: Big Rock Point (ISFSI)
status_note: BWR operated 1962-1997 and is fully decommissioned; only the dry fuel storage installation near Charlevoix remains.
notes: The NRC approved the licence transfer from Entergy to Holtec in 2021; completion of the transfer is not confirmed.

name: Braidwood Station
status_note: Two PWR units in operation (operating licences 1987 and 1988). Spent fuel is stored in the reactor pool(s) and in dry casks at an on-site ISFSI.

name: Browns Ferry Nuclear Plant
status_note: Three BWR units in operation (operating licences 1973-1976). Spent fuel is stored in the reactor pool(s) and in dry casks at an on-site ISFSI.

name: Brunswick Steam Electric Plant
status_note: Two BWR units in operation (operating licences 1974 and 1976). Spent fuel is stored in the reactor pool(s) and in dry casks at an on-site ISFSI.

name: Byron Station
status_note: Two PWR units in operation (operating licences 1985 and 1987). Spent fuel is stored in the reactor pool(s) and in dry casks at an on-site ISFSI.

name: Callaway Plant
status_note: One PWR unit in operation (operating licence 1984). Spent fuel is stored in the reactor pool(s) and in dry casks at an on-site ISFSI.

name: Calvert Cliffs Nuclear Power Plant
status_note: Two PWR units in operation (operating licences 1974 and 1976). Spent fuel is stored in the reactor pool(s) and in dry casks at an on-site ISFSI (site-specific NRC licence).

name: Catawba Nuclear Station
status_note: Two PWR units in operation (operating licences 1985 and 1986). Spent fuel is stored in the reactor pool(s) and in dry casks at an on-site ISFSI.

name: Church Rock uranium mill (United Nuclear Corp.) and Northeast Church Rock Mine
status_note: On 16 July 1979 the tailings dam of the Church Rock mill breached, releasing about 1,000 t of solid tailings and 360,000 m3 of acidic tailings solution into the Puerco River, the largest release of radioactivity in US history. The former mill and tailings area is a Superfund site; clean-up of the adjacent Northeast Church Rock Mine on the Navajo Nation began in July 2026.
notes: The EPA gives both 23 and 26 July 2026 for the groundbreaking.

name: Clinton Power Station
status_note: One BWR unit in operation (operating licence 1987). Spent fuel is stored in the reactor pool(s) and in dry casks at an on-site ISFSI.

name: Clive Disposal Site (EnergySolutions)
status_note: Commercial engineered landfill in Tooele County, Utah, about 60 miles west of Salt Lake City, operating since 1988-1990 (Envirocare, EnergySolutions since 2007). Takes Class A low-level waste, large decommissioning components and, since a 2019 state law, depleted uranium.
notes: Position of Clive community. Sources give 1988 or 1990 as the start year.

name: Columbia Generating Station
status_note: One BWR unit in operation (operating licence 1984). Spent fuel is stored in the reactor pool(s) and in dry casks at an on-site ISFSI.

name: Comanche Peak Nuclear Power Plant
status_note: Two PWR units in operation (operating licences 1990 and 1993). Spent fuel is stored in the reactor pool(s) and in dry casks at an on-site ISFSI.

name: Connecticut Yankee / Haddam Neck (ISFSI)
status_note: PWR operated 1968-1996 and was decommissioned 1998-2007; 40 casks of spent fuel and 3 of GTCC waste stand at the ISFSI on the former plant property.
notes: The storage installation lies about three-quarters of a mile from the former reactor site; the point marks the plant.

name: Cooper Nuclear Station
status_note: One BWR unit in operation (operating licence 1974). Spent fuel is stored in the reactor pool(s) and in dry casks at an on-site ISFSI.

name: Crystal River Unit 3 Nuclear Generating Plant
status_note: Single PWR licensed to operate until 20 February 2013, then decommissioned (DECON). All spent fuel has been in the on-site ISFSI since January 2018.
operator: Accelerated Decommissioning Partners (NorthStar/Orano); spent fuel owned by ADP-SF1, site owned by Duke Energy Florida

name: Davis-Besse Nuclear Power Station
status_note: One PWR unit in operation (operating licence 1977). Spent fuel is stored in the reactor pool(s) and in dry casks at an on-site ISFSI.
notes: NRC sources differ on the licensee: Energy Harbor/FirstEnergy (unit list) or Vistra Operations Company LLC (reactor page, 2026); the latter is used.

name: Diablo Canyon Power Plant
status_note: Two PWR units in operation (operating licences 1984 and 1985). Spent fuel is stored in the reactor pool(s) and in dry casks at an on-site ISFSI (site-specific NRC licence).

name: Donald C. Cook Nuclear Plant
status_note: Two PWR units in operation (operating licences 1974 and 1977). Spent fuel is stored in the reactor pool(s) and in dry casks at an on-site ISFSI.

name: Dresden Nuclear Power Station
status_note: BWR Units 2 and 3 in operation; Unit 1 (1960-1978) is in SAFSTOR and all its fuel has been moved to the on-site ISFSI. Spent fuel is stored in the reactor pool(s) and in dry casks at an on-site ISFSI.

name: Duane Arnold Energy Center
status_note: Single BWR shut down on 10 August 2020; all fuel has been in the on-site ISFSI since April 2022. NextEra is pursuing a restart under NRC review.

name: Edwin I. Hatch Nuclear Plant
status_note: Two BWR units in operation (operating licences 1974 and 1978). Spent fuel is stored in the reactor pool(s) and in dry casks at an on-site ISFSI.

name: Fermi Nuclear Power Plant (Enrico Fermi)
status_note: BWR Unit 2 in operation (operating licence 1985); the fast breeder Fermi 1 (1963-1972) is in SAFSTOR and its fuel was shipped off site in 1973. Spent fuel is stored in the reactor pool(s) and in dry casks at an on-site ISFSI.

name: Fort Calhoun Station
status_note: Single PWR shut down on 24 October 2016 and being dismantled (DECON). All spent fuel has been in the on-site ISFSI since May 2020 and is expected to remain until about 2058.

name: Fort St. Vrain (ISFSI)
status_note: The high-temperature gas-cooled reactor operated 1979-1989; the plant was repowered with natural gas. Its spent fuel is held by DOE at the NRC-licensed Fort St. Vrain ISFSI (SNM-2504) at Platteville.
notes: Position of the generating station; the storage installation is on the same site.

name: Grand Gulf Nuclear Station
status_note: One BWR unit in operation (operating licence 1984). Spent fuel is stored in the reactor pool(s) and in dry casks at an on-site ISFSI.

name: H. B. Robinson Steam Electric Plant
status_note: One PWR unit (Unit 2) in operation (operating licence 1970). Spent fuel is stored in the reactor pool(s) and in dry casks at an on-site ISFSI (site-specific and general NRC licences).

name: HI-STORE consolidated interim storage facility (Holtec, Lea County, cancelled by developer)
status_note: Proposed store for up to 8,680 t of commercial spent fuel in 500 canisters on land of the Eddy-Lea Energy Alliance, roughly halfway between Carlsbad and Hobbs. The NRC issued a licence in May 2023 and the Supreme Court refused a challenge in January 2026, but Holtec cancelled its agreement with ELEA and its plans to build in October 2025.
notes: Position derived from the NRC environmental impact statement (north of US 62/180, next to Laguna Gatuna). The licence still exists; the status reflects the developer withdrawing.

name: Hanford Site
status_note: Former plutonium production complex in Washington State with 177 underground tanks of high-level waste and extensive contamination. The Waste Treatment Plant began vitrifying low-activity tank waste in October 2025 (hot commissioning) and the vitrified containers go to the on-site Integrated Disposal Facility.
waste_types: high-level; transuranic; intermediate-level; low-level; spent-fuel; chemical
operator: US Department of Energy (Office of Environmental Management; contractors incl. Bechtel and Central Plateau Cleanup Company)
notes: The site covers about 1,500 km2; the tank farms on the Central Plateau (200 Areas) are not marked separately.

name: Hope Creek Generating Station
status_note: One BWR unit in operation (operating licence 1986); adjacent to the Salem station. Spent fuel is stored in the reactor pool(s) and in dry casks at an on-site ISFSI.

name: Humboldt Bay (ISFSI)
status_note: BWR Unit 3 operated 1963-1976; plant decommissioning was completed around 2021. Spent fuel and GTCC waste remain in the site-specific ISFSI.

name: Idaho National Laboratory site (INTEC and Radioactive Waste Management Complex)
status_note: Former National Reactor Testing Station with the Idaho Chemical Processing Plant (now INTEC), where spent fuel was reprocessed. The Idaho Cleanup Project ships transuranic waste to WIPP (7,500th shipment April 2025), moves DOE spent fuel into vault storage and operates the Integrated Waste Treatment Unit and an on-site CERCLA disposal facility.
operator: US Department of Energy (Idaho Environmental Coalition for cleanup; Battelle Energy Alliance runs the laboratory)
notes: Position of the INL site, not INTEC itself. INTEC is the former Idaho Chemical Processing Plant, which reprocessed naval and research reactor fuel.

name: Interim Storage Partners consolidated interim storage facility (WCS CISF, proposed)
status_note: Proposed consolidated interim store for commercial spent fuel at the WCS site, licensed by the NRC in September 2021 (docket 72-1050). The Fifth Circuit vacated the licence in 2023, but the US Supreme Court reversed in NRC v. Texas (June 2025) and later challenges were dismissed. No construction is known; Texas state law opposes the project.
operator: Interim Storage Partners (Orano and Waste Control Specialists)
notes: 'Planned' means licensed but not built. Texas state law reportedly opposes the facility.

name: James A. FitzPatrick Nuclear Power Plant
status_note: One BWR unit in operation (operating licence 1974). Spent fuel is stored in the reactor pool(s) and in dry casks at an on-site ISFSI.

name: Joseph M. Farley Nuclear Plant
status_note: Two PWR units in operation (operating licences 1977 and 1981). Spent fuel is stored in the reactor pool(s) and in dry casks at an on-site ISFSI.

name: Kewaunee Power Station
status_note: Single PWR shut down on 7 May 2013 and being decommissioned. All spent fuel was moved from the pool to the on-site ISFSI in 2017.

name: La Crosse Boiling Water Reactor (ISFSI)
status_note: BWR shut down in 1987 and decommissioned; fuel was moved to the ISFSI on the Genoa site in 2012 and the NRC released the rest of the site in 2023, leaving the ISFSI under Dairyland's licence.

name: LaSalle County Station
status_note: Two BWR units in operation. Spent fuel is stored in the reactor pool(s) and in dry casks at an on-site ISFSI.

name: Limerick Generating Station
status_note: Two BWR units in operation (operating licences 1985 and 1989). Spent fuel is stored in the reactor pool(s) and in dry casks at an on-site ISFSI.

name: Los Alamos National Laboratory, TA-54 Area G
status_note: Legacy waste area opened in 1957 with 32 pits, 194 shafts and four trenches of buried radioactive waste. It is now used to store, characterise and remediate legacy transuranic and low-level waste before shipment to WIPP and off-site disposal; buried corrugated metal pipes of TRU waste have been retrieved since 2022.
operator: N3B, for US DOE Environmental Management
notes: Position of the general LANL point; Area G on Mesita del Buey lies several km to the south-east.

name: Maine Yankee (ISFSI)
status_note: PWR operated 1972-1996/97 and was decommissioned 1997-2005; spent fuel and GTCC waste remain in dry casks at the ISFSI on Bailey Point, Wiscasset, awaiting removal by DOE.

name: Massachusetts Bay radioactive waste dumping site
status_note: About 4,000 containers of radioactive waste were dumped at 92 m depth in Massachusetts Bay between 1952 and 1959, according to US data reported to the IAEA.

name: McGuire Nuclear Station
status_note: Two PWR units in operation (operating licences 1981 and 1983). Spent fuel is stored in the reactor pool(s) and in dry casks at an on-site ISFSI.

name: Millstone Power Station
status_note: Two PWR units in operation (operating licences 1975 and 1986); BWR Unit 1 ran 1970-1995/98 and is in SAFSTOR with its fuel kept in the Unit 1 pool. Spent fuel is stored in the reactor pool(s) and in dry casks at an on-site ISFSI.

name: Moab uranium mill tailings pile (Moab UMTRA Project)
status_note: Tailings from the former Atlas uranium mill (1950s-1984) on the bank of the Colorado River are being moved by rail to an engineered disposal cell at Crescent Junction, about 30 miles away; DOE had removed 17 million tons by September 2026, with groundwater clean-up and final stabilisation still to follow.
operator: US Department of Energy, Office of Environmental Management
notes: Position of Moab town; the pile lies a few km north-west of the town on the river. Completion of the Crescent Junction disposal cell is expected in 2029.

name: Monticello Nuclear Generating Plant
status_note: One BWR unit in operation (AEC provisional licence 1970). Spent fuel is stored in the reactor pool(s) and in dry casks at an on-site ISFSI.
operator: Northern States Power Company - Minnesota (Xcel Energy)

name: Morris Operation (GE spent fuel storage, Illinois)
status_note: Away-from-reactor pool store in Grundy County built by General Electric as a reprocessing plant that never operated after 1975 tests. It holds about 772 t of commercial spent fuel; the basins are essentially full and no new fuel is accepted.

name: Nevada National Security Site (former Nevada Test Site)
status_note: About 928 US nuclear tests (100 atmospheric, 828 underground) were carried out here from 1951 to 1992, contaminating groundwater, soils and facilities. DOE's Environmental Management programme is closing groundwater areas with long-term monitoring; Pahute Mesa is the last area still under investigation. The site remains an active NNSA site.
operator: US DOE / NNSA (managed by Mission Support and Test Services LLC)
notes: Radioactive waste disposal facilities on the site are listed separately. The 2028 Pahute Mesa target date is not confirmed.

name: Nevada National Security Site, Area 5 Radioactive Waste Management Site
status_note: Active near-surface disposal site for low-level, mixed low-level and classified waste from approved DOE and DoD sites, including a RCRA-permitted mixed waste unit with liner. Quarterly waste volume reports run to FY2026.
operator: Mission Support and Test Services LLC for the US DOE/NNSA
notes: 'Chemical' stands for mixed (hazardous and radioactive) low-level waste.

name: Nine Mile Point Nuclear Station
status_note: Two BWR units in operation (operating licences 1974 and 1987). Spent fuel is stored in the reactor pool(s) and in dry casks at an on-site ISFSI.
operator: Nine Mile Point Nuclear Station, LLC (Constellation)

name: North Anna Power Station
status_note: Two PWR units in operation (operating licences 1978 and 1980). Spent fuel is stored in the reactor pool(s) and in dry casks at an on-site ISFSI (site-specific and general NRC licences).

name: Oak Ridge Reservation (EMWMF and Environmental Management Disposal Facility)
status_note: Manhattan Project site (Y-12, ORNL) in Tennessee with an on-site cleanup waste disposal facility in operation for about 20 years and nearly full. Construction of the replacement Environmental Management Disposal Facility began in August 2023, with completion planned for 2029; highly contaminated waste is shipped out of state.
operator: US Department of Energy Oak Ridge Office of Environmental Management (UCOR)
notes: Position of Oak Ridge city, not the disposal cells in Bear Creek Valley west of Y-12.

name: Oconee Nuclear Station
status_note: Three PWR units in operation (operating licences 1973-1974). Spent fuel is stored in the reactor pool(s) and in dry casks at an on-site ISFSI (site-specific and general NRC licences).

name: Oyster Creek Nuclear Generating Station
status_note: Single BWR operated 1969-2018 and is being dismantled (DECON). All spent fuel has been in the on-site dry storage ISFSI since May 2021; partial site release excluding the ISFSI is scheduled for 2029.
operator: Holtec Decommissioning International (owner Oyster Creek Environmental Protection, LLC)

name: Palisades Nuclear Plant
status_note: Single PWR shut down in May 2022; in August 2025 it returned to operational licensing status and fuel loading for a restart began in late August 2026, but no restart had been confirmed by mid-October 2026. Spent fuel is stored in the pool and in the on-site ISFSI.
notes: Restart status changes quickly; in October 2026 the NRC approved removal of a tilted fuel assembly after a fuel-loading incident.

name: Palo Verde Nuclear Generating Station
status_note: Three PWR units in operation (operating licences 1985-1987). Spent fuel is stored in the reactor pool(s) and in dry casks at an on-site ISFSI.

name: Peach Bottom Atomic Power Station
status_note: BWR Units 2 and 3 in operation (operating licences 1973 and 1974); the gas-cooled Unit 1 (1967-1974) is in SAFSTOR and its fuel was shipped to a DOE facility in Idaho. Spent fuel is stored in the reactor pool(s) and in dry casks at an on-site ISFSI.

name: Perry Nuclear Power Plant
status_note: One BWR unit in operation (operating licence 1986). Spent fuel is stored in the reactor pool(s) and in dry casks at an on-site ISFSI.
notes: NRC sources differ on the licensee: Energy Harbor/FirstEnergy (unit list) or Vistra Operations Company LLC (reactor page, 2026); the latter is used.

name: Pilgrim Nuclear Power Station
status_note: Single BWR shut down on 31 May 2019 and being decommissioned (DECON). All spent fuel and GTCC waste has been stored in the new ISFSI-II on site since the end of 2021.

name: Point Beach Nuclear Plant
status_note: Two PWR units in operation (operating licences 1970 and 1973). Spent fuel is stored in the reactor pool(s) and in dry casks at an on-site ISFSI.

name: Prairie Island Nuclear Generating Plant
status_note: Two PWR units in operation (operating licences 1974). Spent fuel is stored in the reactor pool(s) and in dry casks at an on-site ISFSI (site-specific NRC licence).
operator: Northern States Power Company - Minnesota (Xcel Energy)

name: Quad Cities Nuclear Power Station
status_note: Two BWR units in operation (operating licences 1972). Spent fuel is stored in the reactor pool(s) and in dry casks at an on-site ISFSI.

name: R. E. Ginna Nuclear Power Plant
status_note: One PWR unit in operation (operating licence 1969). Spent fuel is stored in the reactor pool(s) and in dry casks at an on-site ISFSI.
